records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page for this species is headed Gymnocalycium mihanovichii, and its title parenthetical lists the common names as Chin Cactus, Moon cactus, Plaid Cactus; the page's own description calls the species 'chin cactus', so Chin Cactus is used as the common name. 'Moon cactus' on that page is the shop name for the brightly colored grafted plants: the colored top is a mutant seedling of this species that lacks chlorophyll and is grafted to a host cactus, typically Hylocereus undatus, so the scion depends on its rootstock for nourishment. All care values here are taken from the species page only and nothing was taken from cultivar or rootstock pages.

unknowns: NC State (plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/gymnocalycium-mihanovichii/) is the only admissible source with care values for this species. RHS has a dedicated page (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/248072/gymnocalycium-mihanovichii/details), but it carries only Botanical Details (Family Cactaceae, Name Status Correct, Plant Range Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay) and no sun, soil, moisture, pH or size fields. The MoBot Plant Finder was not reachable, so no care value has a second source to cross-check it.

Toxicity: NC State's page for this species carries no toxicity fields (its Problems field lists only Spines/Thorns), RHS's dedicated page carries none, and ASPCA has no entry, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null.

Rootstock dependence: NC State says the brightly colored grafted plants known as moon cactus have a top that is a mutant seedling of this species, grafted to a host cactus, typically Hylocereus undatus, and that this top (the scion) does not have chlorophyll and relies on the host cactus or rootstock for nourishment. The same page lists Hibotan Nishiki (partial chlorophyll) and Variegata (contains chlorophyll) as able to grow independently. This record holds no care values for the rootstock itself. Cultivar-only traits such as Hibotan being 4 inches tall were not used.

soil_drainage is null. NC State gives a bare Good Drainage rating, asks for well-drained cactus or succulent mix with complete dry-down between waterings, lists Soil Texture as Loam (Silt) and Sand, and warns of fungal disease from overwatering. However, no admissible source calls for sharp or sandy drainage, which the fast token requires, and RHS's dedicated page carries no soil fields.

Temperatures: NC State gives one preferred range of 68 to 86 degrees Fahrenheit without a day/night split, so day_f and night_f fields are null. The advice to bring outdoor plants indoors before temperatures drop below 50 F is a handling instruction, not a damage-onset temperature, so chill_damage_f is null; the page also says the plants are not frost tolerant.

Light: NC State's structured Light field lists Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day) and Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours). The same page says these plants prefer bright, indirect sunlight and warns that overexposure to direct sun can cause scorching, particularly in grafted varieties, so outdoor_sun_exposure keeps part_shade only and full_sun is left out. RHS's dedicated page has no sun fields. direct_sun_hours_max is null because the only hour figures are NC State's generic light-category definitions.

Soil pH: NC State lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0). The acid band is open-ended so no floor is set, and the ceiling of the closed neutral band could not be checked against an RHS pH field, so both soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null.

Watering numbers: no source gives a day interval, check depth or watering basis, so those fields are null. Fertilizer: the page says only to fertilize during the growing season, with no months, interval or strength.

Humidity: the page says low humidity with no percentage, so humidity_pct_min and humidity_pct_max are null. Edibility and pollinator attraction are not addressed by the page, so those fields are null.

Size: NC State's Dimensions block (Height and Width both 0 ft. 2 in. to 0 ft. 3 in., i.e. 2-3 inches) is used for the species itself; the larger 'Hibotan' cultivar figures on the same page were not used.

records.name_note: The dedicated pages split on the name. NC State's Kalanchoe daigremontiana page has the bare binomial as its H1. Its alphabetized Common Name(s) list reads Alligator Plant, Devil's Backbone, Maternity Plant, Mexican Hat Plant and Mother of Thousands, one per line, and its page-title parenthetical reads the same five names in the same order. Its description opens with "Mother of thousands" and says "The name, mother of thousands, is the result of its unusual reproductive method.", so Mother of Thousands is used as the name. RHS's dedicated profile (plant 9674) gives Mexican hat plant beneath its H1 and lists devil's backbone and flopper as other common names; it does not list mother of thousands. NC State lists Bryophyllum daigremontianum as the previous name. NC State's description notes hybrids of this species with the mother of millions (Kalanchoe delagoensis), and its cultivar 'Pink Butterflies' is listed as K. daigremontiana x K. delagoensis; this record is for K. daigremontiana itself, not that hybrid or K. delagoensis.
records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox, K. daigremontiana page. Heading "Poisonous to Humans" (human-scoped block): Poison Severity Medium; Poison Toxic Principle bufadienolides; Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes; Poison Part (full list as rendered): Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Stems. Poison Symptoms as written: "If ingested, symptoms include drooling, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cardiac arrhythmias, and seizures. If pets ingest this plant, it can be a life threatening emergency and possibly fatal. The sap can cause contact dermatitis." The page-top banner, which states no scope, reads "This plant has medium severity poison characteristics." The page's Problems field (separate from the human-scoped severity) lists: Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs. Plant Type tags: Herbaceous Perennial, Houseplant, Poisonous, Succulent. Handling warning (separate from ingestion toxicity): "Protective gloves should be worn when handling this plant due to the risk of contact dermatitis." Also: "If any part of this plant is ingested, it can be toxic to both humans and pets." and "In colder climates, it may be used as a houseplant, but be sure to keep this plant out of the reach of small children and pets." RHS's dedicated profile for this species carries no toxicity information, so NC State is the only admissible source on toxicity and there is no disagreement on scope to report.

unknowns: Sources checked: NC State's dedicated page is the anchor for every value. RHS's dedicated profile (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/9674/kalanchoe-daigremontiana/details) loads, but it supplies no value for a null field and changes none. Its pH row reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', so no bound can be set. Its Moisture row is the bare 'Well–drained'. Its Position row reads 'Full sun' (see outdoor_sun_exposure). Its hardiness rating 'H1B' is a survival rating, not a damage onset. Its Max Height '0.5-1 metres' (about 20-39 in) and Max Spread '0.1-0.5 metres' (about 4-20 in) leave NC State's Dimensions block as the size anchor. Its Cultivation text on compost, watering and feeding is the same text, bar one article, as on RHS's Kalanchoe tomentosa profile, so it is genus-level and not used. It carries no toxicity information. MoBot's Plant Finder could not be read: the sandboxed fetcher fails its TLS certificate chain and the site's firewall blocked a browser search, so whether MoBot has a page for this species is unknown. Clemson HGIC has only a Kalanchoe factsheet about K. blossfeldiana, which does not mention this species; it is not used.

toxic_to_pets=true rests on NC State's Problems field values Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs. Its Poison Symptoms sentence 'If pets ingest this plant, it can be a life threatening emergency and possibly fatal.' names no animal and is carried in toxicity_detail only. NC State's severity (Medium) sits under the human-scoped 'Poisonous to Humans' heading, not a pet-specific rating.
is_edible=false rests on NC State's ingestion warning (toxic to humans and pets); no source says the plant is eaten as food.

soil_drainage left null: NC State's structured Soil Drainage is Good Drainage + Occasionally Dry with Soil Texture Loam (Silt) and Sand, and prose says 'sandy or loamy soil that is well-drained' with a cactus mix; it also warns overwatering can cause root rot, but no source states there is no wet tolerance, so fast is not supported, and a bare well-drained reading is ambiguous.
soil_ph left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), and the open-ended bands give no floor or ceiling.

outdoor_sun_exposure is part_shade only. NC State's structured Light field lists both 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' and 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', and RHS's Position row reads 'Full sun'. full_sun is still left out, because NC State's description says 'This plant prefers bright indirect sunlight or partial shade. It can tolerate some direct sunlight, but it is best to avoid the hot midday sun.' and warns 'Leaf scorch can result if the plant receives prolonged direct sunlight or intense afternoon sun.' RHS's single Position rating does not outweigh that species-specific warning. direct_sun_hours_max is null because the only hour figures are the generic category definitions inside NC State's Light values.

water_regime dry_thoroughly_between is read from 'Allow the soil to dry out between waterings' and 'Water this plant sparingly'; the page does not say 'thoroughly' or give a depth or day interval, so water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est and water_estimate_basis are null. NC State says to reduce watering during the dormant stage but gives no numbers.

Temperature: NC State says the plant 'prefers temperatures between 65 and 75 degrees Fahrenheit', not split into day and night, so day_f and night_f are null. It says the plant is winter hardy in zones 9 to 11 and 'not frost-tolerant', which is a hardiness rating and not a chill-damage onset temperature, so chill_damage_f and cool_rest_note are null.
Humidity, indoor light in foot-candles, fertilizer and pollinator attraction are not addressed on the NC State page, so those fields are null.
Mature size is NC State's Dimensions block (Height 1 ft 0 in - 3 ft 0 in = 12-36 in; Width 1 ft 0 in - 2 ft 0 in = 12-24 in) for this species' own page.
NC State says the plant is monocarpic (dies after flowering) and produces plantlets on leaf margins; this is a care-relevant fact with no schema field.

Two of NC State's names for this plant are also used for other species. Devil's Backbone is in the Common Name(s) list of NC State's Kalanchoe delagoensis page (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/kalanchoe-delagoensis/), which reads Chandelier Plant, Devil's Backbone, Lizard Plant, Mother-In-Law-Plant, Mother of Millons. NC State's Ratibida columnifera page (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/ratibida-columnifera/) lists Mexican Hat, alongside Columnar Prairie Coneflower, Long-headed Coneflower and Prairie Coneflower. Neither name is used as this record's name. 'Millons' is the page's own spelling.

common_name lands as 'Mother Of Thousands': NC State's Description opens with the name and its list carries 'Mother of Thousands', and the landing gate capitalises every word of a landed name, small words included. NC State's alphabetized list opens with Alligator Plant and RHS leads with Mexican hat plant (see name_note). Nothing here is taken from Kalanchoe blossfeldiana (landed as Kalanchoe) or K. tomentosa (Panda Plant).

NC State says it was formerly Rhoeo spathacea; its Previously known as list also carries Rhoeo discolor. records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox page for Tradescantia spathacea, plus the Potentially harmful row on RHS's dedicated profile. NC State's page banner reads 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.' and its 'See below' link points to the 'Poisonous to Humans:' block, which reads: Poison Severity: Low (this severity is human-scoped, from that heading). records.name_note: NC State and RHS each have a dedicated page for Aechmea fasciata. RHS's profile renders urn plant as the subtitle beneath its H1 and lists silver vase plant under Other common names. NC State's page title carries the parenthetical (Silver Vase Bromeliad, Silver Vase Plant, Urn Plant), and its Common Name(s) list renders the same three names in the same alphabetized order, so Silver Vase Bromeliad comes first there; its Description prose opens with "The urn plant or silver vase plant". Urn Plant is used because RHS's subtitle and NC State's Description opener both lead with it. NC State's Aechmea genus page also lists Urn Plant and Silver Vase Plant among its genus-level common names. NC State lists Billbergia fasciata, Bromelia fasciata and Platyaechmea fasciiata (the page's spelling) under Previously known as, so Billbergia fasciata is an old synonym. NC State's "is often confused with" module names Aechmea chantinii.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page for Aechmea fasciata has no Poison block and no toxicity rating. Its Tags block reads: "#vase-shaped #partial shade tolerant #non-toxic for cats #colorful bracts #houseplant #herbaceous perennial #slow growing #drought tolerant #interesting flowers #groundcover #interesting leaves #container plant #spines #mass planting #non-toxic for horses #non-toxic for dogs #epiphytic". The scoping is therefore exactly these tags: non-toxic for cats, non-toxic for dogs and non-toxic for horses. Plant Type values on the page: Epiphyte, Herbaceous Perennial, Houseplant; Appendage: Spines. Handling note (not a toxicity claim): "The margins of the leaf have black spines." RHS's dedicated page for this species carries no toxicity statement, so no admissible source disagrees. Eating the plant is not addressed.
records.water_estimate_basis: NC State's cup routine: keep about 1 inch of water in the central cup continuously, and empty and change that water once a month so it does not stagnate and breed insect pests; watering is reduced during the winter months. No day-interval estimate is derived from this.
unknowns: Three admissible sources have a dedicated Aechmea fasciata page, and every care value in this record is taken from NC State's (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/aechmea-fasciata/). RHS's page is plant 59419 (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/59419/aechmea-fasciata/details), Name Status Correct. Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder page (https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=b647) refuses this machine's non-browser fetches with certificate errors but renders in a browser; the MoBot readings below are the auditor's, no MoBot citation is landed and no value rests on them. RHS's Position ("Partial shade") and MoBot's "Sun: Part shade" agree with part_shade. RHS's Moisture field ("Moist but well–drained") and MoBot's "consistently moist but well-drained soils" agree with moderate drainage. RHS carries the Houseplants label and MoBot calls it a "Good flowering houseplant." MoBot's "Height: 1.00 to 3.00 feet" and "Spread: 1.00 to 2.00 feet" match NC State's Dimensions block. RHS's Max Height and Max Spread both read "0.1-0.5 metres" (about 4-20 inches), smaller than NC State's 12-36 by 12-24 inches; NC State's species Dimensions block is the anchor. Neither RHS nor MoBot addresses toxicity, edibility, humidity or feeding. UF/IFAS's FP014 ("Aechmea spp.: Bromeliad, Aechmea, Vase Plant") covers the genus and was not used.

Bloom-and-die note, captured as stated: NC State says 'It blooms only once and then dies. Offsets or pups form at the base of the parent plant before the parent dies.' It also says the offsets should be 6 inches tall before transplanting.

Temperature: NC State says "The plant thrives in temperatures between 65 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit.", one range with no day/night split. MoBot gives a split, as read by the auditor, "Best performance occurs with indoor temperatures ranging from low 60s F. at night to 75-80 F. during the day.", but its night figure is not a number and its day range runs past NC State's 75 F top, so the sources disagree and day_f and night_f are left null. No source states a cold-damage onset temperature. NC State says only "Brown leaf tips can occur if the plant gets inadequate water or is exposed to cold temperatures.", MoBot (auditor's reading) says "Leaf tips will brown up if soils dry out or plants are grown in areas too cold.", and NC State's USDA Plant Hardiness Zone field (10a, 10b, 11a, 11b) and RHS's H1B rating are hardiness ratings, not onset temperatures, so chill_damage_f is null.

Light: NC State's prose says "This plant prefers bright, indirect light to partial shade." and gives no footcandle figure. outdoor_sun_exposure part_shade comes from NC State's structured Light field (Partial Shade), and RHS's Position ("Partial shade") agrees, as does MoBot's "Sun: Part shade" as read by the auditor. The "2-6 hours" inside NC State's Light value is the Toolbox's standard label for that category, not species prose, so direct_sun_hours_max is null. NC State's USDA Plant Hardiness Zone field reads 10a, 10b, 11a, 11b (MoBot, per the auditor: "Zone: 10 to 11"), and NC State says "In warmer climates, they may be planted outdoors in mass plantings, as a groundcover, or in containers.", so outdoor use applies only in warm climates.

soil_drainage is moderate: NC State's structured Soil Drainage is the bare 'Good Drainage', its prose asks for a 'consistently moist, well-drained' medium, and it warns that overwatering can cause root rot; RHS's structured Moisture field reads 'Moist but well–drained'. Orchid mix is cited only for soil_base orchid_bark, not as evidence of fast drainage. The 'consistently moist' wording could be read as moisture_retentive, but the same-source root-rot warning keeps it at moderate.

water_regime left null: no admissible source gives a watering instruction for the potting medium. NC State's "For houseplants, it requires a consistently moist, well-drained potting medium such as an orchid mix." and MoBot's "consistently moist but well-drained soils" describe the medium (they support soil_drainage moderate, not a watering token), and MoBot's structured "Water: Medium" is mid-scale. The watering statements on both pages concern the central cup and winter: NC State says "It is best to have a small amount (about 1 inch) of water in the central cup continuously." and "Watering should be reduced during the winter months.", and MoBot says "Best with a small pool of water in the central cup formed by the rosette of leaves." and "Reduce watering in winter." Against a wet reading, NC State tags the plant #drought tolerant, lists Drought under Resistance To Challenges and warns "Overwatering can cause root rot.", and MoBot warns "Root rot may occur if soils are kept too moist." NC State's Aechmea genus page, not used for any value, says "As houseplants, they are tolerant of dry air and occasionally dry roots as long as the central tank is kept full of water." No source frames watering as a dry-down, so water_dry_down_target and the day-interval fields are null. Every MoBot sentence here is the auditor's browser reading and is not cited.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0) and Alkaline (>8.0), and the acid and alkaline bands are open-ended.

humidity, fertilizer, edibility and pollinator attraction are not addressed on the NC State page, so those fields are null. is_edible is null (no source addresses eating). The ASPCA entry cannot be checked from admissible sources.
Corpus bromeliads (Guzmania lingulata, Tillandsia ionantha and T. usneoides, Ananas comosus) were not used for any care text.

records.toxicity_detail: Source 1: NC State Plant Toolbox, Dianthus caryophyllus page. Its "Poisonous to Humans" block (human-scoped) gives Poison Severity: Low (the page's summary line reads "This plant has low severity poison characteristics."); Poison Symptoms: "Mild gastrointestinal signs, mild dermatitis"; Poison Toxic Principle: "Unknown irritant". The same block also says Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. That conflicts with the listed symptom of mild dermatitis, and the conflict is recorded here, not resolved. NC State gives no poison-part list, no handling warning and no preparation instructions. Separately, NC State's Problems field (not the human-scoped severity) renders three values: Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses. This supports toxic_to_pets=true because cats and dogs are both named. Co-listed Plant Type values are Annual, Herbaceous Perennial and Perennial. NC State's Edibility field says "Flowers are edible." That is a separate claim with no stated preparation, timing or conditions, and it sits beside the poison block above. Source 2: RHS's dedicated Dianthus caryophyllus page, Potentially harmful field: "Humans/Pets: Skin allergen; wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants". This handling warning agrees with NC State's mild dermatitis symptom and disagrees with NC State's Causes Contact Dermatitis: No; the two sources disagree and the disagreement is recorded, not resolved. RHS's "Humans/Pets" scope names no animal species. RHS says nothing about eating the plant.

The MoBot, plantfinder.mobot.org and Clemson pages could not be loaded (ConnectError / HTTP 403). Where RHS bears on the record: its Position field renders only "Full sun"; its Moisture field reads "Well–drained" and its pH field "Neutral or Alkaline", which neither makes soil_drainage fast nor sets a pH ceiling; its Max Height "0.5-1 metres" (19.7-39.4 in) and Max Spread "0.1-0.5 metres" (3.9-19.7 in) differ from NC State's Dimensions block (12-48 in by 6-12 in), which stays the size anchor; its Potentially harmful field carries the handling warning recorded in toxicity_detail.

Heat intolerance, as NC State states it: "Carnations are intolerant of high heat and might be a poor choice for the southern garden." The page also says they prefer cooler summer climates. It gives no temperature figures, so day/night temperature fields and chill_damage_f are null. The listed USDA zones 6a-9b are a hardiness range, not a damage-onset temperature.

Toxicity conflict inside NC State's poison block: Poison Symptoms lists "mild dermatitis" but the same block says Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Both are recorded, neither resolved. The toxic principle is given as an unknown irritant. No poison-part list is given. Severity Low comes from the human-scoped Poisonous to Humans block. The Problem for Cats / Dogs / Horses tags are a separate Problems field with no severity. RHS's Potentially harmful field calls the plant a skin allergen and advises gloves, which disagrees with NC State's Causes Contact Dermatitis: No.

is_edible is null, not true (landing decision under the catalog's edibility rule). NC State's Edibility field reads "Flowers are edible.", its Flower Value To Gardener field lists Edible, its Landscape Theme field lists Edible Garden and its tag row carries #edible flowers; no preparation, timing or condition is given. The same page rates the plant low-severity poisonous under its Poisonous to Humans block (Poison Symptoms "Mild gastrointestinal signs, mild dermatitis", Poison Toxic Principle "Unknown irritant", no poison part named, so the flowers are not excluded) and lists it as a Problem for Cats, Dogs and Horses, and RHS calls it a skin allergen. A one-line statement that the flowers of an ornamental and cut flower are edible, on a page that rates the plant poisonous, is a marginal food use, so the record does not show the plant as grown to eat. water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, the day-interval fields and water_estimate_basis are null. The page has no watering statement. Its Moist soil-drainage tag and the "moist, well-drained" soil wording describe soil, not a watering regime, and no source frames watering as a dry-down cycle.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. NC State's dedicated Phedimus spurius page has the page-title parenthetical (Creeping Stonecrop, Stonecrop, Two-row Stonecrop) and an alphabetized Common Name(s) list in the same order, so Creeping Stonecrop is listed first and Two-row Stonecrop third; its body prose uses the bare name Stonecrop. RHS's dedicated Phedimus spurius page is titled with Caucasian stonecrop and renders it beneath its H1, and its separate Other common names field lists crimson stonecrop and large fringed stonecrop. Caucasian Stonecrop is used, following RHS, whose Sedum spurium page leads with the same name. On naming, NC State heads the page Phedimus spurius and lists Sedum spurium under Previously known as. RHS's Phedimus spurius page shows Name Status Synonym and a Genus field describing Sedum, and its Sedum spurium page shows Name Status Correct, so RHS files the plant under Sedum and the sources disagree on the accepted name; the accepted name here follows NC State's dedicated page. Dragon's Blood, Fuldaglut and Tricolor are cultivars listed on NC State's page, not separate species.
records.toxicity_detail: Toxicity and edibility conflict on NC State's page and both keep their conditions. NC State's Poisonous to Humans block (human-scoped, not a cat or dog statement) gives Poison Severity Low; the page also says "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." Poison Symptoms: "Unknown, but possibly gastrointestinal symptoms." Poison Toxic Principle: "Alkaloids sedine, sedamine, and others." Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part: Flowers, Leaves, Roots, Stems. NC State's Plant Type field lists three values together: Ground Cover, Herbaceous Perennial, Poisonous. On the other side, NC State's Edibility field says: "Stems and leaves, when very young and tender, may be eaten raw. Later, until they flower, they may be briefly cooked." That edibility statement is conditional (very young and tender, raw; later until flowering, briefly cooked), and the stems and leaves it calls edible are on NC State's own Poison Part list, so this record does not mark the plant edible (is_edible is left null). NC State's page carries no Problem for Cats or Problem for Dogs tags, and RHS gives no toxicity information, so there is no cat/dog evidence.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: NC State's poison block is headed Poisonous to Humans and the page has no Problem for Cats or Problem for Dogs tags; RHS's page carries no toxicity information, nor, as read by the auditor in a browser, does MoBot's; no page read names cats or dogs.

is_edible is null, not true (landing decision under the catalog's edibility rule). NC State's Edibility field reads 'Stems and leaves, when very young and tender, may be eaten raw. Later, until they flower, they may be briefly cooked.' The same page lists Poisonous among its Plant Type values and carries a low-severity Poisonous to Humans block (Poison Symptoms 'Unknown, but possibly gastrointestinal symptoms.', Poison Toxic Principle 'Alkaloids sedine, sedamine, and others.', Poison Part Flowers, Leaves, Roots, Stems), so the stems and leaves the Edibility field calls edible are on its own poison-part list. Eating the young shoots of a poisonous ornamental ground cover is a marginal food use, so the record does not show the plant as grown to eat; the Edibility sentence stays cited under toxicity_detail.

Light: NC State's structured Light field lists only Partial Shade, but its own description says the plant requires full sun. RHS's structured Position field reads Full sun, and MoBot's Sun field, as read by the auditor, reads Full sun with light shade only tolerated. So outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only, and part_shade is left out and disclosed here. RHS's Cultivation paragraph is genus-level Sedum text (identical on its Sedum ternatum page) and is not used. direct_sun_hours_max left null because NC State's only hour range is the site-wide legend inside the structured field.

MoBot's dedicated page (Sedum spurium, taxonid=279381) fails certificate verification for non-browser fetches but renders in a browser, where the auditor read it. It leads with Caucasian stonecrop, is headed Sedum spurium, gives full sun with light shade tolerated, and says 'Leaves are arranged in two rows along the stems, hence the sometimes used common name of two row stonecrop.' Its quotes cannot be checked mechanically, because verify_quotes skips plantfinder.mobot.org, so no MoBot citation is landed.

soil_drainage fast: NC State says it requires well-drained, sandy or shallow rocky soil and prefers very dry soil. RHS's structured Moisture field reads Moist but well-drained or Well-drained, a milder counterpoint; the NC State text is the species-specific watering and soil statement and no source wants wet soil.

water_regime dry_thoroughly_between rests on NC State's 'Do not overwater, as it prefers very dry soil'; RHS's Moist but well-drained or Well-drained field is a mid-scale counterpoint and gives no watering instruction. No interval or dry-down figure is stated, so those fields are null.
soil_base left null: no admissible source names a potting or bed mix.
soil_ph left null: RHS lists Alkaline or Neutral, which is open-ended on the alkaline side, and NC State gives no pH.

Name: the admissible sources disagree. NC State treats Phedimus spurius as current, with Sedum spurium as the former name. RHS treats the plant as Sedum spurium: its Phedimus spurius page shows Name Status Synonym and a Genus field describing Sedum, and its Sedum spurium page shows Name Status Correct. MoBot's page is headed Sedum spurium, as read by the auditor. The given name is kept and follows NC State.

Temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles, fertilizing and chill damage have no figure in the admissible pages read; NC State lists hardiness zones 3a-9b and RHS H5, which are not damage-onset temperatures.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page (Insects, Diseases, and Other Plant Problems paragraph) says: "All parts of this plant are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses." NC State's tag list carries "#problem for dogs #problem for horses #problem for cats", and its Problems field lists Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses. NC State's Plant Type is Herbaceous Perennial. The page has no Poison block (so no human-poison information, no poison-part list and no severity rating), gives no symptom list and no handling warning. The cat, dog and horse scope comes only from that sentence and those tags. This is Hosta, not Lilium, and no Lilium toxicity data is carried over. The admissible pages do not address edibility. RHS's dedicated page for this species carries no toxicity statement.
unknowns: Full sun: NC State's structured Light field lists Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day) alongside Dappled Sunlight, Deep shade and Partial Shade, but its prose says the plant 'thrives in sites with deep to partial shade' and that 'Locations with full sun may be used as planting sites in cooler climates, providing proper moisture is maintained.', a condition on full sun, and RHS's structured Position field reads 'Full shade, Partial shade'. full_sun is therefore left out of outdoor_sun_exposure and the cooler-climate-with-moisture condition is recorded here. NC State also says 'It is the most heat and sun tolerant of the hosta species', a comparison within the genus, not a full-sun recommendation. NC State's Dappled Sunlight value is mapped to part_shade and its Deep shade value to full_shade.

soil_drainage is moderate from NC State's Good Drainage + Moist pair, the NC State prose 'moist soils with good drainage', and RHS's 'moist but well-drained' (its Cultivation sentence, which differs from its Hosta sieboldiana page's, and its structured Moisture field).
